Newly hatched Draughtsboard sharks (Cephaloscyllium isabellum) emerge from their egg cases at a remarkably small size, with a total length at birth of just 16 centimeters [Lb = 16 centimeters]. This diminutive size at parturition is consistent with the general pattern observed among many scyliorhinid species, where offspring are born as fully formed miniature adults after a prolonged period of internal yolk dependence. Field records suggest that the young pups, once they begin independent foraging, must navigate a challenging environment dominated by larger predators and limited prey resources. The initial growth phase following this exotrophic transition is characterized by a relatively slow accumulation of body mass, as the juveniles allocate much of their ingested energy toward structural development and the acquisition of foraging skills. Studies of captive-born individuals indicate that the first several months of life are critical for establishing a robust feeding ecology, with the pups gradually shifting from a diet of small benthic invertebrates to larger, more elusive prey items such as small teleost fishes. This ontogenetic dietary shift is a common feature among demersal elasmobranchs and is likely linked to the progressive development of jaw musculature and sensory capabilities.

As the juvenile Draughtsboard shark continues to grow, it eventually reaches a critical developmental milestone: the onset of sexual maturation. For females, puberty is attained at a total length of 76.1 centimeters [Lp = 76.1 centimeters], a size that reflects the considerable energetic investment required for gonad maturation and eventual gestation. Males, in contrast, achieve reproductive maturity at a significantly smaller body size, with total length at puberty recorded at 60.3 centimeters [Lp = 60.3 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in size at maturity is a widespread phenomenon among sharks and is often attributed to the differing selective pressures acting on the two sexes: females benefit from a larger body cavity to support developing embryos, whereas males can commence reproductive activity earlier, thereby increasing their lifetime mating opportunities. Data derived from tag-recapture studies and vertebral band counts indicate that the transition from immature organism to sexually viable adult encompasses a period of several years, during which the sub-adults continue to refine their predatory strategies and expand their home ranges.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the species' deep-water, temperate habitat in New Zealand, a consistent body of physiological measurements has been compiled. At a water temperature of 11.8 °C [T = 11.8 °C], the gestation period for this species extends for approximately 13 months, corresponding to an age at birth of 396.5 days [ab = 396.5 days]. This protracted developmental interval, during which the yolk-dependent embryo undergoes organogenesis and growth within the egg case, is likely an adaptive response to the cooler waters that slow metabolic processes. Furthermore, at the same ambient temperature, the maximum reproductive rate for female Draughtsboard sharks has been estimated at two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year], with each litter typically comprising a single pup [N_R_i = each litter typically comprising a single pup]. This frequency of pupping events is relatively high for a shark of its body size and may be facilitated by the species' ability to store sperm from a single copulation event, allowing females to fertilize successive clutches of eggs without the need for repeated insemination.

The ultimate total length attained by this species has been documented at 108 centimeters [Li = 108 centimeters], a body size that places Cephaloscyllium isabellum among the larger members of its genus. Correlating with this maximum length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult has been calculated at approximately 8030 grams [Wwi = approximately 8030 grams], a mass that reflects the robust, somewhat rotund body form for which the Draughtsboard shark is named. This body mass estimate, derived from a length-weight relationship based on a morphometric formula, underscores the significant energetic costs associated with maintaining somatic tissues in a cold-water environment. Adult individuals exhibit a relatively slow, ambush-based foraging strategy, relying on their cryptic coloration and ability to inflate their bodies with water or air as a defensive mechanism against potential predators. The comparison between the juvenile mass at birth and this adult asymptote highlights the substantial growth trajectory that must be completed before the onset of reproductive activity.

The life history of the Draughtsboard shark is completed over a moderate timescale, with the maximum lifespan in the wild recorded at approximately 15.5 years [am = approximately 15.5 years] when measured at a consistent environmental temperature of 11.8 °C [T = 11.8 °C]. This longevity is typical for a demersal elasmobranch of its size and is consistent with the species' relatively slow maturation and modest annual reproductive output. The period of reproductive senescence, if it occurs, appears to be brief, with most adults remaining reproductively active until close to the time of natural mortality. The ultimate factor limiting lifespan is often a combination of physiological deterioration and the increasing difficulty of securing prey as the animal ages, leading to a gradual loss of body condition. Comparative analyses with other members of the family Scyliorhinidae suggest that the trade-off between early maturation and extended lifespan is finely balanced in this lineage, with the cooler, stable temperatures of the continental slope environment favoring a slower pace of life over a more rapid life cycle.
